title: Whoever wins the election, Israel’s illiberal turn is here to stay – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: ECFR's Beth Oppenheim argues that regardless of who wins Israel's October 27th election, a hardline religious-right elite has driven an illiberal turn that will persist, with prolonged coalition instability likely and little change in security doctrine.

insights.claim: Polls show Eisenkot's Yashar! at 22 seats narrowly ahead of Likud at 20, with Netanyahu's bloc averaging 51 and the opposition 52, so neither reaches the 61 of 120 Knesset seats needed.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: Points to prolonged instability and possible re-run elections.

insights.claim: The opposition needs the ultra-Orthodox or Palestinian citizen parties to govern, and both have signalled openness at a price, but Jewish opposition leaders rule out both.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: Coalition math, not vote share, determines the outcome.
insights.locator: Given that the opposition is likely to fall short

insights.claim: Five scenarios include deadlock with Netanyahu as caretaker until spring 2027 elections, an Eisenkot minority government backed by Palestinian citizen parties or the ultra-Orthodox, defector poaching, or a rotating national unity government more likely in a security emergency such as renewed war with Iran.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: Expect months of political uncertainty in Israel.

insights.claim: A hardline religious-right elite has embedded itself in key institutions and is remaking Israel toward a Greater Israel in which Jewish law trumps liberal democracy, so even an opposition government will not restore liberal democratic credentials.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: Long-run Israeli institutional drift is not election-dependent.

insights.claim: Netanyahu's post-October 7th security doctrine of pre-emption, operating beyond borders and holding buffer zones is embraced by nearly all Jewish Israeli parties, and a former senior official said differences between Netanyahu and Eisenkot 'are very minor'.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: Do not expect foreign policy regime change from a new government.

insights.claim: An Eisenkot government would be fragile but would halt the judicial overhaul, open a state inquiry into October 7th, pass a conscription law, ease Gaza disarmament demands and curb settler violence, while still expanding settlements.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: Better odds for Gaza ceasefire phase two under an opposition government.

insights.claim: Without a diplomatic track with the Palestinians, normalisation with Saudi Arabia stays off the table and flare-ups in the West Bank and Gaza are inevitable.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: Abraham Accords expansion is unlikely near term.

insights.claim: Europeans should set out conditions privately for resetting ties with the new government and, if it does not change course, be ready to use political and economic leverage such as measures against the settlement project, a task complicated by possible European illiberal gains in 2027.
insights.speaker: Beth Oppenheim
insights.so_what: Raises prospect of EU measures on settlements.
